Where MLLMs Fail and Why: Causal Task Decomposition for Capability Failure Diagnosis

Xia Hu Affiliation: \thepa    Brian Potetz Affiliation: \thepa    Chun-Ta Lu Affiliation: Google Research    Huanfen Yao Affiliation: \thepa    Leonidas Guibas Affiliation: \thepa Affiliation: Stanford University    Zhicheng Wang Affiliation: \thepa    Howard Zhou Affiliation: \thepa    Pengfei Xing Affiliation: \thepa    Andrew Gallagher Affiliation: \thepa
Abstract

End-to-end accuracy on compositional tasks records how often MLLMs fail, but cannot distinguish whether a failure reflects an intrinsic deficit in the targeted capability or a cascading error from an upstream prerequisite. We propose a causal decomposition framework that isolates these two failure modes through controlled interventions on the prerequisite dependencies of each task. Our capability metrics (NC, IC, RC) score each task under unassisted, correct, or incorrect prerequisites to diagnose where failures arise; contribution metrics (N-Score, S-Score), adapted from probabilities of causation, quantify each prerequisite’s necessity and sufficiency to determine why. We instantiate the framework in CADET, a diagnostic benchmark of 10 composite tasks decomposed into 46 unit tasks with over 33,000 human-annotated questions spanning perception, spatial, temporal, and cognitive categories. Diagnosing frontier MLLMs with our framework uncovers systematic patterns that end-to-end accuracy obscures. Capability-wise, supplying correct prerequisites eliminates 54% of errors on cognitive tasks, lifting them from weakest to above spatial and temporal. Prerequisite-wise, causal contributions are concentrated in a few critical prerequisites, and supplying the single most important one alone captures 84% of the gain from supplying all prerequisites.

1 Introduction

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly evaluated on compositional tasks requiring multiple interdependent capabilities, from perceiving objects and estimating spatial layouts to tracking over time and reasoning [48, 46]. Such tasks are typically scored by a single end-to-end accuracy, which records how often a model fails but not where its failures originate. The score conflates an intrinsic deficit, where the model lacks the targeted capability, with a cascading error, where it possesses that capability but fails on an upstream prerequisite. In Fig 1, a model failing on multi-view sequential may lack temporal reasoning or merely misjudge the camera viewpoint on which ordering depends, yielding the same error but opposite capability diagnoses. More broadly, low accuracy on high-level cognitive tasks is naturally read as a reasoning deficit, a reading that holds only if the perceptual and spatial steps beneath it are sound, and growing evidence suggests they often are not [8, 39].

A common response examines the constituent steps directly, by decomposing the task into separately scored sub-questions [31, 52] or inspecting the reasoning trace for the first erroneous step [21]. Both localize failure more finely than an aggregate score, yet observing untreated generation alone cannot disentangle the two failure modes. First, a model’s generated reasoning trace or answers to isolated sub-questions need not reflect what it relies on to solve the full task [40, 5]. Second, even a faithful readout reveals only co-occurrence: a prerequisite failing alongside the final task neither shows how much final failure is attributable to it, nor answers the counterfactual had it been solved correctly. Indeed, the outcome need not hinge on the weakest prerequisite: in Fig 1, standalone accuracy is lowest for task-5, yet final performance turns on task-2. Input-level interventions do move beyond observation, supplying ground-truth intermediates [23] or injecting false premises [17], but each tests a single condition, without a dependency structure linking sub-tasks or a measure of each prerequisite’s contribution. What is missing is an evaluation setting every prerequisite’s state within a shared, explicit dependency structure, so that the same controlled contrasts apply across capabilities and models, and each prerequisite’s contribution is measured rather than inferred.

We propose a causal decomposition framework that turns MLLM evaluation from observation into a controlled experiment. We decompose each task into unit tasks with explicit prerequisite dependencies, and intervene on each by supplying a correct answer, an incorrect answer, or nothing. To diagnose where failures arise, we define natural, intrinsic, and resilience capability (NC, IC, RC) under these three prerequisite states, isolating a model’s performance on a target task from the influence of its modeled prerequisites. To explore why the overall outcome fails, we introduce the NN-Score and SS-Score, which measure each prerequisite’s causal necessity and sufficiency for the final outcome: the fraction of success lost when it alone is degraded, and the fraction of failure recovered when it alone is supplied. These metrics adapt classical probabilities of causation [38, 29] to the LLM setting without assuming monotonicity, providing valid lower bounds on the probabilities of necessity and sufficiency.

To instantiate this framework, we introduce CADET, a multimodal diagnostic benchmark in which each complex task is decomposed via an explicit structural causal model (SCM) into unit tasks that each target a single capability, and every unit-task question is annotated with both a verified correct answer and a plausible incorrect answer to enable three-state interventions. The benchmark spans 10 tasks, yielding 46 unit tasks and over 33,000 unit-task questions across four capability categories: perception, spatial, temporal, and cognitive. All questions and annotations are newly created by human annotators to mitigate data contamination and assure benchmark quality.

Evaluation on 12 frontier MLLMs exposes diagnostic patterns that end-to-end accuracy obscures. At capability level, cognitive tasks scores lowest naturally (NC=0.41\text{NC}{=}0.41) yet rises to second under correct prerequisites (IC=0.72\text{IC}{=}0.72), eliminating 54%54\% of its natural errors; whereas spatial and temporal still retain 7272–75%75\% of their error, locating the more persistent capability gaps there. Injecting incorrect prerequisites degrades all models on perception and spatial (RC<NC\text{RC}{<}\text{NC}) yet improves cognitive in 10 of 12 models. Turning to causal contributions, NN- and SS-Scores reveal effective bottleneck sparsity, where a few critical prerequisites drive each task, and that a corrupted prerequisite costs far more than an omitted one. The single highest-SS prerequisite alone captures 84%84\% full-prerequisite gain, and rarely coincides with the lowest-NC prerequisite. Model-wise exhibits distinct diagnostic profiles, especially, the top four achieve close intrinsic capabilities (IC) despite differing in NC, and pair lower degradation loss (NN) with higher supply recovery (SS) than others. Together, our work moves MLLM evaluation beyond scoring how often models fail to diagnosing where and why they fail.

2 Related Work

Multimodal Evaluation and Task Decomposition. Existing benchmarks evaluate MLLMs across broad capability taxonomies [48, 22, 53], while specialized suites target individual skills such as perception and spatial [8, 46] or vary visual and textual inputs to test modality reliance [39, 49]. Beyond evaluating tasks as a whole, one line of work decomposes complex problems into sub-questions and compares sub-task accuracy with overall performance [31, 52]. Another inspects a model’s generated reasoning steps to locate where errors first occur [21, 50], though recent studies show that stated chains-of-thought do not always reflect the computation behind the final answer [40, 5]. Both read out the model’s unassisted behavior, linking sub-task and final correctness by co-occurrence; we instead set each prerequisite to a known correct or incorrect state.

Causal Interventions for Model Diagnosis. Causal interventions are used to diagnose MLLMs and LLMs by modifying specific components at inference time to measure their effect on outputs, such as patching internal activations [25, 44] or perturbing visual and textual modalities [20, 19]. For multi-step reasoning, recent studies apply step-level interventions to execution traces, editing intermediate outputs or re-executing trajectories to identify failure-inducing steps [24, 41, 2, 35]. At task-input level, prior studies provide ground-truth intermediate results to isolate downstream reasoning [23, 36] or inject false premises to test robustness under misleading context [17, 26]. These interventions either operate on model internals or single-run trajectories, or test one input condition in isolation; ours act on a task-defined causal graph shared across models.

Quantifying Prerequisite Contributions. Attributing MLLM behavior to individual components often involves distinguishing whether a factor is necessary to prevent failure or sufficient to drive success, a distinction formalized by counterfactual necessity and sufficiency [29, 38] and adopted in explainable AI for feature-level attribution [42, 9]. In LLMs, recent studies adapt these causal concepts to test whether responses on synthetic logic problems conform to the ground-truth rules of the queries [14], or to add missing and prune redundant chain-of-thought steps [47]. Both operate on the model’s own outputs; we instead attribute final-task outcomes to prerequisite via necessity and sufficiency.

3 Causal Decomposition Framework

3.1 Task Decomposition via Structural Causal Models

Each evaluation task is decomposed into unit tasks testing a single constituent capability, with directed dependencies where some tasks rely on the outcomes of others. We represent these dependencies as a structural causal model (SCM) [28, 30], leveraging the established framework of causal interventions for the analysis below.

Definition 3.1 (Task Decomposition SCM).

Consider an evaluation task decomposed into nn constituent capabilities. A task decomposition is a structural causal model (SCM) over unit task variables X1,X2​…,XnX_{1},X_{2}\ldots,X_{n}, where XiX_{i} denotes the outcome of unit task ii, given by the structural assignment:

Xi:=fi(Pa(Xi),Ni),i=1,…,n,\small X_{i}\;:=\;f_{i}\!\bigl(\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i}),\;N_{i}\bigr),\hskip 9.24994pti=1,\ldots,n, (1)

where fif_{i} is the structural function determining XiX_{i}, Pa⁡(Xi)⊆{X1,…,Xn}\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i})\subseteq\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\} is the parents set of XiX_{i}, and NiN_{i} is a noise variable capturing unmodeled factors such as the model’s sampling stochasticity.

Root nodes (those with Pa⁡(Xi)=∅\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i}){=}\emptyset) represent foundational capabilities that can be assessed independently, while the final node Y:=XnY{:=}X_{n} corresponds to the overall task outcome.

3.2 Causal Intervention Design

To disentangle intrinsic capability from cascading upstream influence, and quantify each capability’s causal role, we adopt the interventionist framework of causal inference [29, 28, 34] and introduce a ternary intervention scheme tailored to LLM evaluation.

Definition 3.2 (Ternary Intervention).

For unit task XiX_{i}, we define an intervention Ai=aA_{i}{=}a, a∈{1,0,∅}a{\in}\{1,0,\varnothing\}: (i) Ai=1A_{i}{=}1 denotes injecting the correct answer for XiX_{i} into the prompt; (ii) Ai=0A_{i}{=}0 denotes injecting an incorrect answer for XiX_{i}; (iii) Ai=∅A_{i}{=}\varnothing denotes the natural state where XiX_{i} is not injected.

Notation. All probabilities are induced by a fixed model ℳ\mathcal{M}, whose subscript we suppress. We write 𝒜:={1,0,∅}\mathcal{A}{:=}\{1,0,\varnothing\} for the ternary intervention space. For a unit task set SS and a∈𝒜a{\in}\mathcal{A}, we write d​o​(𝐀S=a)do(\mathbf{A}_{S}{=}a) for the homogeneous intervention placing every Xj∈SX_{j}{\in}S in state aa, and abbreviate 𝐀−i:=𝐀Pa⁡(Y)∖{Xi}\mathbf{A}_{-i}{:=}\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(Y){\setminus}\{X_{i}\}}.

Notably, the distinction between Ai=∅A_{i}{=}\varnothing, Ai=0A_{i}{=}0 is critical: the former preserves the model’s natural execution path by evaluating it unassisted, where the latter imposes an active counterfactual intervention testing reasoning under a false premise. Since LLM evaluation operates through input manipulation rather than passive observation, this ternary formulation emerges as the natural space of interventions, allowing us to systematically evaluate model behavior across each pairwise contrast of states.

Assumption 3.3 (Exogeneity under Intervention-Only Identification).

In LLM evaluation setting, the state of a unit task Xi∈{1,0}X_{i}\in\{1,0\} admits no faithful observational readout and is identified only through the intervention Ai=aA_{i}{=}a. Consequently, probabilities conditioning on Xi=xX_{i}{=}x for x∈{1,0}x\in\{1,0\} are identified with the corresponding interventional probabilities:

P(⋅∣Xi=x)=P(⋅∣do(Ai=x)).\small P(\cdot\mid X_{i}=x)\;=\;P(\cdot\mid\operatorname{do}(A_{i}=x)). (2)
Remark 3.4 (Justification).

Assumption 3.3 follows from the LLM evaluation setting: the state of XiX_{i} admits no faithful observational readout [40, 5], thus a reliable mechanism to place XiX_{i} in a determinate state x∈{1,0}x{\in}\{1,0\} is to inject the corresponding answer into the prompt, making conditioning on Xi=xX_{i}{=}x and intervening do⁡(Ai=x)\operatorname{do}(A_{i}=x) operationally identical. This condition coincides with the exogeneity assumption P⁡(yx)=P⁡(y∣x)P(y_{x}){=}P(y\mid x) of Pearl [29], Tian and Pearl [38], but with an inverted justification: classical exogeneity invokes the absence of confounders to treat observations as interventions, whereas ours follows from the absence of a faithful observational channel making intervention the reliable state-assignment mechanism.

3.3 Capability Metrics

With the ternary intervention mechanism established, we can now place the prerequisites Pa⁡(Xi)\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i}) of any target task XiX_{i} into controlled states and measure how the model’s performance on XiX_{i} responds. By additionally evaluating under do⁡(𝐀Pa⁡(Xi)=1)\mathrm{do}(\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i})}{=}1) and do⁡(𝐀Pa⁡(Xi)=0)\mathrm{do}(\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i})}{=}0), we isolate the model’s capability on XiX_{i} when its declared prerequisites are correctly provided versus actively corrupted.

Definition 3.5 (Causal Capability).

Let XiX_{i} be any task node in the SCM with prerequisite dependencies Pa⁡(Xi)\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i}). For an intervention state a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, the causal capability of ℳ\mathcal{M} on XiX_{i} is

Cap⁡(Xi,a):=P⁡(Xi=1∣d​o​(𝐀Pa⁡(Xi)=a)),\small\mathrm{Cap}(X_{i};a):=P\big(X_{i}{=}1\mid do(\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i})}{=}a)\big), (3)

i.e., the probability that ℳ\mathcal{M} solves XiX_{i} when all of its prerequisites are placed in state aa. This yields three complementary metrics: (i) natural capability NC⁡(Xi):=Cap⁡(Xi,∅)\mathrm{NC}(X_{i}):=\mathrm{Cap}(X_{i};\varnothing), the natural performance where no prerequisite is injected; (ii) intrinsic capability IC⁡(Xi):=Cap⁡(Xi,1)\mathrm{IC}(X_{i}):=\mathrm{Cap}(X_{i};1), the performance isolated from declared prerequisites; and (iii) resilience capability RC⁡(Xi):=Cap⁡(Xi,0)\mathrm{RC}(X_{i}):=\mathrm{Cap}(X_{i};0), the robustness under corrupted prerequisite context.

For root nodes (Pa⁡(Xi)=∅\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i}){=}\emptyset), no upstream intervention applies and only NC⁡(Xi)\mathrm{NC}(X_{i}) is defined. For non-root nodes, the three metrics disentangle a model’s proficiency on XiX_{i} from the influence of modeled prerequisites. Specifically, comparing IC⁡(Xi)\mathrm{IC}(X_{i}) with NC⁡(Xi)\mathrm{NC}(X_{i}) separates two failure modes: a large gap IC⁡(Xi)−NC⁡(Xi)\mathrm{IC}(X_{i}){-}\mathrm{NC}(X_{i}) indicates that the model can solve XiX_{i} given correct prerequisites, pointing to upstream cascading errors as the primary bottleneck; a small gap with low IC⁡(Xi)\mathrm{IC}(X_{i}) suggests an intrinsic deficit on XiX_{i} even when all modeled prerequisites are satisfied. Finally, comparing RC⁡(Xi)\mathrm{RC}(X_{i}) with NC⁡(Xi)\mathrm{NC}(X_{i}) shows whether false prerequisites mislead the model below its natural baseline, or still help guide its reasoning despite being factually wrong.

3.4 Contribution Metrics: N-Score and S-Score

Building on node-level capability diagnostics, understanding how upstream unit tasks across the SCM affect the final outcome YY requires quantifying their causal contributions. To formalize this causal attribution, we draw upon the probabilities of causation framework [29, 38], which evaluates counterfactual causal influence through the Probability of Necessity (PN\mathrm{PN}) and Probability of Sufficiency (PS\mathrm{PS}). We do not assume monotonicity: in LLM reasoning, injecting incorrect answer (Ai=0A_{i}{=}0) can help more than no injection (Ai=∅A_{i}{=}\varnothing), so RC\mathrm{RC} may exceed NC\mathrm{NC} (Sec 5.2).

Property 3.6 (Absence of Monotonicity).

Under the LLM evaluation setting, the causal effect of intervening on a unit task XiX_{i} via AiA_{i} on downstream outcome task YY is not assumed to satisfy monotonicity. That is, the natural ordering below is not required to hold in general:

P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=0))≤P⁡(Y=1)≤P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=1)).\small P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}0))\leq P(Y{=}1)\leq P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}1)). (4)

Without monotonicity, exact PN\mathrm{PN} and PS\mathrm{PS} values cannot be determined from interventional probabilities alone, so we introduce the N-Score and S-Score as observable lower bounds to capture the causal contribution of each prerequisite Xi∈Pa⁡(Y)X_{i}\in\mathrm{Pa}(Y) to the final outcome YY:

Definition 3.7 (N-Score).

Let YY be a target outcome task with prerequisite dependencies Pa⁡(Y)\mathrm{Pa}(Y), let Xi∈Pa⁡(Y)X_{i}\in\mathrm{Pa}(Y), and let (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}) be a pair of distinct states in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The N-Score of XiX_{i} on YY is

N(a,a′)​(Xi,Y):=max⁡{0,P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(𝐀Pa⁡(Y)=a))−P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=a))P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(𝐀Pa⁡(Y)=a))},\footnotesize\mathrm{N}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y):=\max\left\{0,\;\frac{P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(Y)}{=}a)\big)-P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}a)\big)}{P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(Y)}{=}a)\big)}\right\}, (5)

measuring the fraction of YY’s success under state aa harmed by degrading XiX_{i} alone from aa to a′a^{\prime}.

Definition 3.8 (S-Score).

Under the setting of Definition 3.7, the S-Score of XiX_{i} on YY is

S(a,a′)​(Xi,Y):=max⁡{0,P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a,𝐀−i=a′))−P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(𝐀Pa⁡(Y)=a′))1−P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(𝐀Pa⁡(Y)=a′))},\footnotesize\mathrm{S}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y):=\max\left\{0,\;\frac{P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}a^{\prime})\big)-P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(Y)}{=}a^{\prime})\big)}{1-P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(Y)}{=}a^{\prime})\big)}\right\}, (6)

measuring the fraction of YY’s failure under state a′a^{\prime} recovered by upgrading XiX_{i} alone from a′a^{\prime} to aa.

Theorem 3.9.

Under Assumption 3.3 and Property 3.6, N-Score and S-Score provide valid lower bounds on the Probability of Necessity (PN\mathrm{PN}) and Probability of Sufficiency (PS\mathrm{PS}).

Specifically, N-Score quantifies causal necessity by measuring how much of the model’s success on YY depends on XiX_{i}. A high N-Score pinpoints critical performance bottlenecks where one degraded task breaks overall success even when all other prerequisites remain at aa. Conversely, S-Score quantifies causal sufficiency by measuring how much of the model’s failure on YY can be overcome through XiX_{i}. A high S-Score identifies high-leverage prerequisites where supplying a single task rescues overall success even when other prerequisites remain at a′a^{\prime}. Setting the other prerequisites 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i} asymmetrically to aa for N-Score and a′a^{\prime} for S-Score aligns with realistic evaluation by testing single-task vulnerability under favorable prerequisite conditions and single-task rescue under degraded ones, making the two metrics complementary rather than directly convertible [29]. We provide the general definitions of N-Score, S-Score under arbitrary 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i} and theoretical discussions in Appendix.

In practice, we evaluate N-Score and S-Score across four ordered state contrasts (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}) over 𝒜={1,0,∅}\mathcal{A}{=}\{1,0,\varnothing\}: (1,0)(1,0), (1,∅)(1,\varnothing), (∅,0)(\varnothing,0), and (0,∅)(0,\varnothing). As summarized in Tab 1, the first two contrasts measure both degradation from prerequisite corruption or omission and recovery through targeted correction or repair, whereas the latter two evaluate both directions between ∅\varnothing and 00 to capture either misinformation harm or structural scaffolding under Property 3.6. Together, our node-level capability metrics (NC,IC,RC\text{NC},\text{IC},\text{RC}) and edge-level contribution metrics (N-Score,S-Score\text{N-Score},\text{S-Score}) form a causal diagnostic framework for complex multimodal tasks, which we instantiate in Sec 4.

4 Benchmark

To apply the causal decomposition framework to frontier MLLMs and uncover where and why they fail, we construct CADET, a multimodal benchmark where complex tasks are decomposed into unit tasks connected via SCM and every prerequisite admits controlled interventions (details in Appendix).

Benchmark Overview. CADET comprises 10 multimodal evaluation tasks across over 1,100 instances, decomposed into 46 atomic unit tasks and over 33,000 unit-task questions, with both overall and their constituent unit tasks categorized into four core capabilities: perception, spatial, temporal, and cognitive. To operationalize our causal framework, each overall task is paired with an explicit SCM defining its prerequisite structure, and every unit task is annotated with both a correct and an incorrect answer, along with visual annotations on the images where applicable, to support the ternary intervention scheme (Ai∈{1,0,∅}A_{i}{\in}\{1,0,\varnothing\}) at every node. The multimodal inputs span single, multi-images and videos, while the outputs use structured formats (multiple-choice, integer, or list) for 43 of the 46 tasks and free-form text for the remaining three.

Task Design and SCM Structure. Tasks are drawn primarily from real-world scenarios and designed as compositional problems requiring interdependent capabilities on which frontier MLLMs are far from saturation, so that diagnosis targets gaps these models still face. We further cover diverse input modalities, application domains, and capability compositions, from foundational perception to high-level cognitive reasoning. For each task, we formalize the prerequisite dependencies among its unit tasks into an SCM (Fig 2). These structures range from shallow aggregations (e.g., Dice Sum) to deep multi-path cascades (e.g., Traffic Causation). In decomposition, we identify unit tasks that involve iterative solving of structurally recurring sub-problems, where each step depends on the previous step’s outcome and reasoning depth itself becomes a variable; we define these as Markov chain unit tasks. In the task-level SCM, a Markov chain unit task participates as a single node; for finer-grained analysis, we unfold it into a step-wise chain to track how capabilities evolve with reasoning depth. Tasks whose primary structure is a Markov chain are analyzed separately in Sec 5.4.

Data Construction and Quality Assurance. All evaluation content, including questions, answers, and unit-task annotations, is newly created by an experienced rater pool to mitigate data contamination; source images and videos are drawn from publicly available datasets with permissive licenses (e.g., Wilson et al. [43]). The benchmark is constructed in two stages: raters first generate overall task questions and ground-truth answers under predefined task definitions. Based on each task’s SCM, we decompose its unit tasks into standardized atomic annotation tasks, such as bounding box localization and semantic labeling. Raters provide the corresponding visual annotations and ground-truth labels, which are then converted into unit-task questions and correct answers via structured templates, ensuring consistent alignment between all evaluation items and the underlying causal structure. Incorrect answers are randomly sampled from the valid answer space rather than manually crafted, providing a standardized, model-independent perturbation. To ensure benchmark quality, each annotation across both stages is independently verified by a quality-check rater who returns deficient items for iterative revision until acceptance. Beyond per-item verification, instances flagged as ambiguous or un-annotatable are removed during final assembly to ensure reliable causal diagnosis.

5 Experiments and Findings

5.1 Experiment Setting

Evaluated Models. We evaluate 12 frontier MLLMs across six model families, covering both proprietary series: Gemini [12], GPT [27], Grok [45]; and open-weight series: Gemma [6], Qwen [32], Kimi [37]. This selection encompasses different model families at varying capability scales, enabling both cross-family and within-family diagnostic comparisons. All models are queried through public APIs with default parameter setting. Thinking mode is set to high or left at its default if not-configurable.

Intervention Implementation. To operationalize the ternary intervention, for each prerequisite unit task XiX_{i}, we inject its intervened state (Ai∈{1,0}A_{i}{\in}\{1,0\}) into prompt as a structured JSON question-answer pair. For Ai=1A_{i}{=}1, alongside the correct textual answer, we render corresponding visual annotations (e.g., bounding box, path) whenever the prerequisite’s ground truth directly represents spatial information in the scene. For Ai=0A_{i}{=}0, incorrect answer is injected via text without modifying the image, to prevent shifting the visual referent of the query and ensure we test reasoning under a false premise about the intended target. Under natural state Ai=∅A_{i}{=}\varnothing, no prerequisite information is provided for XiX_{i}.

Evaluation Protocol. We report the capability metrics (NC, IC, RC) for each unit task, and the contribution metrics (N-Score, S-Score) on the overall task across four state contrasts: (1,0)(1,0), (1,∅)(1,\varnothing), (∅,0)(\varnothing,0), and (0,∅)(0,\varnothing). Model predictions are evaluated via exact match for structured outputs, with Gemini 3.6 Flash serving as LLM judger [51] for free-form text tasks and format mismatches. Full experimental settings are provided in Appendix.

5.2 Capability Diagnostics

Cascading errors reorder the apparent capability ranking. Under end-to-end evaluation (NC), accuracy falls across perception, spatial, temporal, and cognitive tasks (0.59, 0.56, 0.46, 0.41; Fig 5(a)), a pattern that would attribute the largest deficits to high-level reasoning. Supplying correct prerequisites (IC) reorders the categories: cognitive reasoning moves to second (0.72), above spatial (0.67) and temporal (0.61), behind only perception (0.80). Decomposing the total error into a cascading component IC−NC\mathrm{IC}{-}\mathrm{NC} and a residual component 1−IC1{-}\mathrm{IC} accounts for this shift, as cascading errors constitute 54% of cognitive failures (0.32 of 0.59). Spatial and temporal reasoning show the opposite composition, with residual errors (0.33, 0.39) covering 75% and 72% of their failures and small gains from correct prerequisites (0.12, 0.15), locating the more persistent intrinsic capability gaps at these two categories rather than at cognition.

Frontier models share similar intrinsic ceilings but differ in cascading errors (Fig 5(b-e)). Supplying correct prerequisites (IC) brings the top 4 SOTA models to nearly identical ceilings across categories (0.88-0.91 in perception, 0.80-0.83 in cognition), tracing their end-to-end (NC) gaps to cascading errors (IC−NC\mathrm{IC}{-}\mathrm{NC}): GPT-5.4 and Gemini family trade places, with larger cascading loss for GPT-5.4 in perception (0.28 vs. 0.15–0.22) and for Gemini in cognition (0.35–0.37 vs. 0.24). Across all 12 models, perception exhibits the widest spread in residual errors (1−IC1{-}\mathrm{IC}: 0.09–0.45), spatial shows uniformly high residual errors (0.25–0.43), and cognitive carries uniformly large cascading errors (IC−NC\mathrm{IC}{-}\mathrm{NC}: 0.22–0.37). Model-wise, close NC scores mask divergent error compositions: Qwen3.5 397B and Kimi K2.5 match neighboring models in NC yet carry substantially higher residual errors (1−IC1{-}\mathrm{IC}) in different categories.

Incorrect prerequisites harm perception and spatial but mildly aid cognition. The RC−NC\text{RC}{-}\text{NC} gap rises across the hierarchy (Fig 5): all 12 models fall below zero in perception and spatial, while 10 of 12 turn positive in cognition. The gap also varies widely across models within each category (−0.28-0.28 to +0.12+0.12). The positive cognitive gaps directly instantiate the non-monotonicity formalized in Property 3.6: incorrect prerequisites do not uniformly degrade performance.

5.3 Causal Contribution Analysis

Causal contributions exhibit effective bottleneck sparsity. Evaluating prerequisite contributions via N⁡(1,∅)N(1,\varnothing) and S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) (Fig 5) across 8 non-Markov tasks shows that causal influence is highly uneven across parents, with each task driven by one or a few critical prerequisites. These critical parents act either as core bottlenecks that cause large oracle drops when omitted and strong natural recovery when provided (high NN/high SS), or as compensable levers whose omission is offset by other oracle prerequisites yet still rescue natural failures alone (low NN/high SS). By contrast, the remaining prerequisites have individually small effects (low NN/low SS), while conjunctive bottlenecks that hurt oracle performance without aiding natural recovery are nearly absent (high NN/low SS).

Disaggregating by model reveals two distinct criticality patterns. Expanding to individual models (Fig 6) reveals two task patterns and a broad split between top-4 (SOTA) and remaining (Others) models. Under Pattern 1 (Fig 6a,b), both groups exhibit critical prerequisites with high single-point recovery capacity (high SS), with Others shifting moderately toward higher NN and lower SS. Under Pattern 2 (Fig 6c,d), SOTA keeps prerequisites at high SS with low oracle omission sensitivity (low NN), whereas Others shift substantially toward higher NN and lower SS, losing effective single-point recoverability while suffering larger oracle drops from single-task omission. Across both patterns, SOTA maintains low oracle vulnerability and often has multiple high-SS prerequisites per task that each could rescue natural failures alone; while Others drift rightward and downward, moderately in Pattern 1 and severely in Pattern 2, reflecting higher oracle sensitivity and weaker single-task recovery. Structurally, the prerequisite count |Pa⁡(Y)||\mathrm{Pa}(Y)| averages 3.0 in Pattern 1 and 5.25 in Pattern 2.

A single supplied prerequisites recovers most full-prerequisite gains. Supplying only the single most sufficient prerequisite (max⁡S⁡(1,∅)\max S(1,\varnothing)) recovers 84% of the full all-prerequisite gain (IC−NC\mathrm{IC}{-}\mathrm{NC}) overall (Fig 8b), showing that one targeted intervention already accounts for most of the attainable gain. This leverage is not readable from standalone accuracy: S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) does not track NC⁡(Xi)\mathrm{NC}(X_{i}) across prerequisites (Fig 8a). To test whether cheaper node-level signals could substitute for S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) in identify the same prerequisite, we repeat single-parent repair under alternative criteria (including the weakest prerequisite min⁡(NC)\min(\mathrm{NC}); Fig 8b), none of which recovers this single-parent optimum overall. The shortfall of NC\mathrm{NC} stays around 8 pp in Pattern 1 tasks, where models share a single dominant bottleneck; but widens sharply in Pattern 2 tasks with denser multi-parent dependencies, where S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing)-chosen parent sustains 76% of the full gain while NC\mathrm{NC}-based only 36%.

Incorrect prerequisites hurt far more than omission. Extending to full ternary contrast space (Fig 8,10), injecting incorrect prerequisites is consistently more destructive than leaving them unassisted (N⁡(1,0)>N⁡(1,∅)N(1,0){>}N(1,\varnothing) across all categories), with minor gains from incorrect answers on temporal (S⁡(0,∅)=0.071S(0,\varnothing){=}0.071). Unlike cognitive target tasks benefiting from incorrect prerequisites (Sec 5.2), the two cognitive prerequisites are highly sensitive to correctness: corrupting or omitting them causes the steepest overall task drops (N⁡(1,0),N⁡(1,∅)N(1,0),N(1,\varnothing)) with no gain from incorrect answers (S⁡(0,∅)S(0,\varnothing)), while fixing or removing them drives strong recovery (S⁡(1,0),S⁡(∅,0)S(1,0),S(\varnothing,0)). SOTA models (Fig 8) pair uniformly lower NN with higher SS than Others across all four contrasts, showing stronger robustness to single-prerequisite degradation with superior single-point recovery even under corruption.

5.4 Markov Chain Unit Task Analysis

We analyze the Markov chain unit tasks (Sec 4), in which each XtX_{t} depends solely on its predecessor Xt−1X_{t-1}. Under this single-parent structure, N, S-Score converge into a single NS-Score (N​S​(a,a′)=N⁡(a,a′)⋅Cap⁡(Xt,a){NS}(a,a^{\prime}){=}{N}{(a,a^{\prime})}{\cdot}\mathrm{Cap}(X_{t};a); Appendix). Fig 10 reports NC\mathrm{NC}, IC\mathrm{IC}, RC\mathrm{RC} and N​SNS score along step tt. First, capability degrades nonlinearly with a single-step effective horizon: in goal-directed tasks, IC\mathrm{IC} and N​S​(1,∅){NS}(1,\varnothing) remain flat until one step from the exit (Fig 10b, t=10t{=}10); symmetrically, in process-cumulative tasks where NC\mathrm{NC} collapses to a flat floor immediately at t=1t{=}1, IC\mathrm{IC} and N​S​(1,∅){NS}(1,\varnothing) peak at the first step (Fig 10c) and gradually decline with depth. Second, alternating Position (Fig 10c) and Action (Fig 10d) nodes within the same chain respond divergently to incorrect prerequisites: N​S​(0,∅)≈0{NS}(0,\varnothing){\approx}0 for spatial tracking versus substantial for action planning, consistent with the finding in Sec 5.2 that incorrect prerequisites benefit cognitive reasoning but not perception. Third, as depth tt grows, Position continues to require factual correctness (N​S​(0,∅)≤0.06≪NS​(1,∅){NS}(0,\varnothing)\leq 0.06\ll\text{NS}(1,\varnothing)), whereas in cognitive Action, N​S​(0,∅){NS}(0,\varnothing) steadily rises from 0.120.12 (t=1t{=}1) to 0.300.30 (t≥14t{\geq}14) to match NS​(1,∅)\text{NS}(1,\varnothing) (RC≈IC\text{RC}{\approx}\text{IC}), showing that explicit prerequisite conditioning, regardless of correctness, increasingly accounts for cognitive recovery at deeper horizons.

6 Conclusion

We introduced a causal decomposition framework and the CADET benchmark, applying controlled ternary interventions over explicit prerequisite structures to diagnose where and why MLLMs fail. Our capability metrics (NC, IC, RC) separate cascading influence from intrinsic deficits, showing that supplying correct prerequisites substantially lifts cognitive tasks while spatial and temporal reasoning retain persistent intrinsic gaps, and that incorrect prerequisites often still aid cognition. The NN-, SS-Scores reveal effective bottleneck sparsity, where a few critical prerequisites drive each task, and supplying the single most sufficient one recovers most full-prerequisite gain yet rarely coincides with the least accurate prerequisite. Across models, top ones exhibit lower degradation alongside stronger single-point recovery. More broadly, our diagnostic framework can inform future improvements, from inference-time CoT guidance, query rewriting to training and multi-step system design.
