Appendix A Details and Proofs of Causal Decomposition Framework

In this section, we provide the general definitions of N-Score and S-Score under arbitrary prerequisite states, followed by the theoretical proofs and properties of our causal decomposition framework.

The do-operator. We adopt the standard do-operator (Section 3.2; Pearl [28]). For a∈{1,0}a\in\{1,0\}, d​o​(Ai=a)do(A_{i}{=}a) replaces the structural assignment of XiX_{i} in (1) with Xi:=aX_{i}:=a while keeping all other assignments unchanged, and d​o​(Ai=∅)do(A_{i}{=}\varnothing) leaves the assignment of XiX_{i} intact; interventions on multiple unit tasks apply these operations jointly. P(⋅∣do(⋅))P(\cdot\mid do(\cdot)) denotes the distribution induced by the resulting SCM.

A.1 General Definition of N-Score, S-Score

In Section 3.4 (Definitions 3.7 and 3.8), when quantifying the causal contribution of a prerequisite unit task Xi∈Pa⁡(Y)X_{i}\in\mathrm{Pa}(Y) to the target outcome YY across an ordered contrast (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}), we specifically set the remaining prerequisites 𝐀−i:=𝐀Pa⁡(Y)∖{Xi}\mathbf{A}_{-i}:=\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(Y)\setminus\{X_{i}\}} to the homogeneous state aa for N-Score and a′a^{\prime} for S-Score. Here, we generalize this formulation by allowing the remaining prerequisites to take any arbitrary intervention state configuration.

Specifically, let 𝐜∈𝒜|Pa⁡(Y)∖{Xi}|\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{A}^{|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)\setminus\{X_{i}\}|} denote an arbitrary intervention state configuration assigned to 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i}, denoted as d​o​(𝐀−i=𝐜)do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}=\mathbf{c}), which sets the intervention state of each prerequisite Xj∈Pa⁡(Y)∖{Xi}X_{j}\in\mathrm{Pa}(Y){\setminus}\{X_{i}\} to Aj=cjA_{j}=c_{j} with cj∈𝒜c_{j}\in\mathcal{A}. Following the notation in Section 3.2, when all unit tasks in 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i} are placed in a single homogeneous state c∈𝒜c\in\mathcal{A} (i.e., cj=cc_{j}=c for all Xj∈Pa⁡(Y)∖{Xi}X_{j}\in\mathrm{Pa}(Y){\setminus}\{X_{i}\}), we write d​o​(𝐀−i=c)do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}=c) without boldface. Based on this general state configuration 𝐜\mathbf{c} for the remaining prerequisites, we define the general N-Score and S-Score as follows.

Definition A.1 (General N-Score).

Let YY be a target outcome task with prerequisite dependencies Pa⁡(Y)\mathrm{Pa}(Y), let Xi∈Pa⁡(Y)X_{i}\in\mathrm{Pa}(Y), and let (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}) be an ordered pair of distinct states in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. For any intervention state configuration 𝐜∈𝒜|Pa⁡(Y)∖{Xi}|\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{A}^{|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)\setminus\{X_{i}\}|} assigned to the remaining prerequisites 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i}, the general N-Score of XiX_{i} on YY is defined as:

N(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜):=max⁡{0,P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a,𝐀−i=𝐜))−P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=𝐜))P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a,𝐀−i=𝐜))},\small\mathrm{N}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}):=\max\left\{0,\,\frac{P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})\big)-P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})\big)}{P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})\big)}\right\}, (7)

measuring the fraction of YY’s success under d​o​(Ai=a,𝐀−i=𝐜)do(A_{i}{=}a,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}) that is lost when XiX_{i} alone is degraded from aa to a′a^{\prime}.

Definition A.2 (General S-Score).

Under the setting of Definition A.1, for any intervention state configuration 𝐜∈𝒜|Pa⁡(Y)∖{Xi}|\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{A}^{|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)\setminus\{X_{i}\}|} assigned to 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i}, the general S-Score of XiX_{i} on YY is defined as:

S(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜):=max⁡{0,P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a,𝐀−i=𝐜))−P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=𝐜))1−P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=𝐜))},\small\mathrm{S}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}):=\max\left\{0,\,\frac{P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})\big)-P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})\big)}{1-P\big(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})\big)}\right\}, (8)

measuring the fraction of YY’s failure under d​o​(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=𝐜)do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}) that is recovered when XiX_{i} alone is upgraded from a′a^{\prime} to aa.

Under these general definitions, the N-Score (Definition 3.7) and S-Score (Definition 3.8) introduced in Section 3.4 correspond to the special cases where every element of 𝐜\mathbf{c} is set to the homogeneous state cj=ac_{j}=a (i.e., d​o​(𝐀−i=a)do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}=a)) for N-Score and cj=a′c_{j}=a^{\prime} (i.e., d​o​(𝐀−i=a′)do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}=a^{\prime})) for S-Score, respectively.

A.2 Lower Bound Guarantee of N-Score and S-Score

This section provides the formal statement and proof of Theorem 3.9 in Section 3.4. We establish the lower-bound guarantee for the general N-Score and S-Score (Definitions A.1 and A.2) under an arbitrary prerequisite configuration 𝐜\mathbf{c} (Theorems A.3 and A.4), where Theorem 3.9 corresponds to the special cases 𝐜=a\mathbf{c}=a for N-Score and 𝐜=a′\mathbf{c}=a^{\prime} for S-Score.

Theorem A.3.

Under Assumption 3.3 (Exogeneity), for any prerequisite unit task Xi∈Pa⁡(Y)X_{i}\in\mathrm{Pa}(Y), any ordered contrast (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}) of distinct states in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and any intervention state configuration 𝐜∈𝒜|Pa⁡(Y)∖{Xi}|\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{A}^{|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)\setminus\{X_{i}\}|} assigned to the remaining prerequisites 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i}, the general N-Score (Definition A.1) provides a valid lower bound on the Probability of Necessity (PN\mathrm{PN}) under prerequisite context d​o​(𝐀−i=𝐜)do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}):

PN(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)≥N(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)\small\mathrm{PN}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\geq\mathrm{N}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}) (9)

In particular, setting every element of 𝐜\mathbf{c} to the homogeneous state aa (i.e., d​o​(𝐀−i=a)do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}a)) directly establishes the N-Score lower bound in Theorem 3.9.

Proof.

Note that under exogeneity and non-monotonicity, the mathematical technique of bounding probabilities of causation via Fréchet inequalities [7] is established in the foundational works of Pearl [29], Tian and Pearl [38], Pearl [28], Balke and Pearl [1]. Here, we adapt and instantiate their derivation step-by-step to demonstrate how it applies to our multi-parent LLM evaluation setting under prerequisite configuration d​o​(𝐀−i=𝐜)do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}), Assumption 3.3, and Property 3.6.

For notational conciseness under the prerequisite intervention d​o​(𝐀−i=𝐜)do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}), in below proof, let P𝐜(⋅):=P(⋅∣do(𝐀−i=𝐜))P_{\mathbf{c}}(\cdot):=P(\cdot\mid do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})) denote the probability measure in the induced submodel ℳ𝐜\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{c}} [28], where YaY_{a} and Ya′Y_{a^{\prime}} denote the potential outcomes of YY under further regime interventions d​o​(Ai=a)do(A_{i}{=}a) and d​o​(Ai=a′)do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime}) within ℳ𝐜\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{c}}. Following Pearl [29], the Probability of Necessity (PN\mathrm{PN}) across contrast (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}) under context 𝐜\mathbf{c} is defined as the counterfactual probability that YY fails under d​o​(Ai=a′)do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime}), given that YY succeeded under regime Ai=aA_{i}{=}a:

PN(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜):=P𝐜​(Ya′=0∣Ai=a,Y=1)\small\mathrm{PN}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}):=P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0\mid A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)

If P𝐜​(Ai=a,Y=1)=0P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)=0, the success baseline is zero and the bound holds trivially by convention (N(a,a′)=0\mathrm{N}_{(a,a^{\prime})}=0). Thus, assuming P𝐜​(Ai=a,Y=1)>0P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)>0, we first apply the definition of conditional probability:

P𝐜​(Ya′=0∣Ai=a,Y=1)=P𝐜​(Ya′=0,Ai=a,Y=1)P𝐜​(Ai=a,Y=1)\small P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0\mid A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)=\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0,\,A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)}

By the consistency property of structural causal models, the observed outcome under regime Ai=aA_{i}{=}a coincides with the potential outcome YaY_{a}. Substituting Y=YaY=Y_{a} into the numerator yields:

P𝐜​(Ya′=0∣Ai=a,Y=1)=P𝐜​(Ya′=0,Ai=a,Ya=1)P𝐜​(Ai=a,Y=1)\small P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0\mid A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)=\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0,\,A_{i}{=}a,\,Y_{a}{=}1)}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)}

Next, we factor out the marginal regime probability P𝐜​(Ai=a)P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a) in the numerator and divide both the numerator and the denominator by it:

P𝐜​(Ya′=0∣Ai=a,Y=1)=P𝐜​(Ya′=0,Ya=1∣Ai=a)​P𝐜​(Ai=a)P𝐜​(Ai=a,Y=1)=P𝐜​(Ya′=0,Ya=1∣Ai=a)P𝐜​(Y=1∣Ai=a)\small\begin{split}P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0\mid A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)&=\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0,\,Y_{a}{=}1\mid A_{i}{=}a)\,P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a)}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)}\\ &=\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0,\,Y_{a}{=}1\mid A_{i}{=}a)}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y{=}1\mid A_{i}{=}a)}\end{split}

Under the exogeneity of the regime assignment (Assumption 3.3), the potential outcomes (Ya,Ya′)(Y_{a},Y_{a^{\prime}}) are independent of AiA_{i}, and conditioning on AiA_{i} is operationally identical to intervening on it. This removes the conditioning event in both the numerator and the denominator:

P𝐜​(Ya′=0∣Ai=a,Y=1)=P𝐜​(Ya′=0,Ya=1)P𝐜​(Ya=1)\small P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0\mid A_{i}{=}a,\,Y{=}1)=\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0,\,Y_{a}{=}1)}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)}

Since we do not assume monotonicity (Property 3.6) in LLM reasoning, the joint counterfactual probability P𝐜​(Ya′=0,Ya=1)P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0,\,Y_{a}{=}1) cannot be point-identified from marginal probabilities alone. Applying the classical Fréchet lower bound P𝐜​(E1,E2)≥max⁡{0,P𝐜​(E1)+P𝐜​(E2)−1}P_{\mathbf{c}}(E_{1},E_{2})\geq\max\{0,\,P_{\mathbf{c}}(E_{1})+P_{\mathbf{c}}(E_{2})-1\} [29] to the numerator gives:

PN(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)≥max⁡{0,P𝐜​(Ya′=0)+P𝐜​(Ya=1)−1P𝐜​(Ya=1)}\small\mathrm{PN}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\geq\max\left\{0,\,\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0)+P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)-1}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)}\right\}

Using the complement rule P𝐜​(Ya′=0)=1−P𝐜​(Ya′=1)P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0)=1-P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}1) gives:

PN(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)≥max⁡{0,P𝐜​(Ya=1)−P𝐜​(Ya′=1)P𝐜​(Ya=1)}\small\mathrm{PN}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\geq\max\left\{0,\,\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)-P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}1)}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)}\right\}

Finally, unpacking the submodel notation back into full interventional probabilities via P𝐜​(Ya=1)=P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a,𝐀−i=𝐜))P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)=P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a,\,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})) and P𝐜​(Ya′=1)=P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=𝐜))P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}1)=P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})) yields:

PN(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)\displaystyle\mathrm{PN}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}) ≥max⁡{0,P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a,𝐀−i=𝐜))−P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=𝐜))P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a,𝐀−i=𝐜))}\displaystyle\geq\max\left\{0,\,\frac{P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a,\,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}))-P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}))}{P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a,\,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}))}\right\}

Thus

PN(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)\displaystyle\mathrm{PN}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}) ≥N(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜).\displaystyle\geq\mathrm{N}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}).

∎

Theorem A.4.

Under Assumption 3.3 (Exogeneity), for any prerequisite unit task Xi∈Pa⁡(Y)X_{i}\in\mathrm{Pa}(Y), any ordered contrast (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}) of distinct states in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and any intervention state configuration 𝐜∈𝒜|Pa⁡(Y)∖{Xi}|\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{A}^{|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)\setminus\{X_{i}\}|} assigned to the remaining prerequisites 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i}, the general S-Score (Definition A.2) provides a valid lower bound on the Probability of Sufficiency (PS\mathrm{PS}) under prerequisite context d​o​(𝐀−i=𝐜)do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}):

PS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)≥S(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)\small\mathrm{PS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\geq\mathrm{S}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}) (10)

In particular, setting every element of 𝐜\mathbf{c} to the homogeneous state a′a^{\prime} (i.e., d​o​(𝐀−i=a′)do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}a^{\prime})) directly establishes the S-Score lower bound in Theorem 3.9.

Proof.

Similar to the proof of Theorem A.3, let P𝐜(⋅):=P(⋅∣do(𝐀−i=𝐜))P_{\mathbf{c}}(\cdot):=P(\cdot\mid do(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})) denote the probability measure in the submodel ℳ𝐜\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{c}}, where YaY_{a} and Ya′Y_{a^{\prime}} represent the potential outcomes of YY under d​o​(Ai=a)do(A_{i}{=}a) and d​o​(Ai=a′)do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime}). Following Pearl [29], the Probability of Sufficiency (PS\mathrm{PS}) across contrast (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}) under context 𝐜\mathbf{c} measures the counterfactual probability that upgrading XiX_{i} to state aa would rescue YY to success, given that YY failed under regime Ai=a′A_{i}{=}a^{\prime}:

PS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜):=P𝐜​(Ya=1∣Ai=a′,Y=0)\small\mathrm{PS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}):=P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1\mid A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)

If P𝐜​(Ai=a′,Y=0)=0P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)=0, the failure baseline is zero and the bound holds trivially by convention (S(a,a′)=0\mathrm{S}_{(a,a^{\prime})}=0). Thus, assuming P𝐜​(Ai=a′,Y=0)>0P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)>0, we expand this conditional counterfactual probability using the definition of conditional probability:

P𝐜​(Ya=1∣Ai=a′,Y=0)=P𝐜​(Ya=1,Ai=a′,Y=0)P𝐜​(Ai=a′,Y=0)\small P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1\mid A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)=\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1,\,A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)}

By consistency, the observed outcome under regime Ai=a′A_{i}{=}a^{\prime} coincides with the potential outcome Ya′Y_{a^{\prime}}, so we replace the observed failure Y=0Y{=}0 in the numerator with Ya′=0Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0:

P𝐜​(Ya=1∣Ai=a′,Y=0)=P𝐜​(Ya=1,Ai=a′,Ya′=0)P𝐜​(Ai=a′,Y=0)\small P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1\mid A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)=\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1,\,A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0)}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)}

Factoring out P𝐜​(Ai=a′)P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime}) in the numerator and dividing both the numerator and the denominator by it yields:

P𝐜​(Ya=1∣Ai=a′,Y=0)=P𝐜​(Ya=1,Ya′=0∣Ai=a′)​P𝐜​(Ai=a′)P𝐜​(Ai=a′,Y=0)=P𝐜​(Ya=1,Ya′=0∣Ai=a′)P𝐜​(Y=0∣Ai=a′)\small\begin{split}P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1\mid A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)&=\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1,\,Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0\mid A_{i}{=}a^{\prime})\,P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime})}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)}\\ &=\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1,\,Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0\mid A_{i}{=}a^{\prime})}{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y{=}0\mid A_{i}{=}a^{\prime})}\end{split}

Under the exogeneity of the regime assignment (Assumption 3.3), the potential outcomes (Ya,Ya′)(Y_{a},Y_{a^{\prime}}) are independent of AiA_{i}, and conditioning on AiA_{i} is operationally identical to intervening on it. This removes the conditioning event in both the numerator and the denominator:

P𝐜​(Ya=1∣Ai=a′,Y=0)=P𝐜​(Ya=1,Ya′=0)1−P𝐜​(Ya′=1)\small P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1\mid A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,Y{=}0)=\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1,\,Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0)}{1-P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}1)}

Since monotonicity is not assumed (Property 3.6), the joint counterfactual probability P𝐜​(Ya=1,Ya′=0)P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1,\,Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0) is again not point-identified. Applying the Fréchet lower bound P𝐜​(Ya=1,Ya′=0)≥max⁡{0,P𝐜​(Ya=1)+P𝐜​(Ya′=0)−1}P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1,\,Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0)\geq\max\{0,\,P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)+P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0)-1\} [29] to the numerator yields:

PS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)≥max⁡{0,P𝐜​(Ya=1)+P𝐜​(Ya′=0)−11−P𝐜​(Ya′=1)}\small\mathrm{PS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\geq\max\left\{0,\,\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)+P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0)-1}{1-P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}1)}\right\}

Substituting P𝐜​(Ya′=0)=1−P𝐜​(Ya′=1)P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0)=1-P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}1) into the numerator simplifies the fraction to:

PS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)≥max⁡{0,P𝐜​(Ya=1)−P𝐜​(Ya′=1)1−P𝐜​(Ya′=1)}\small\mathrm{PS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\geq\max\left\{0,\,\frac{P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)-P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}1)}{1-P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}1)}\right\}

Finally, unpacking the submodel notation P𝐜​(Ya=1)=P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a,𝐀−i=𝐜))P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)=P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a,\,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})) and P𝐜​(Ya′=1)=P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=𝐜))P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}1)=P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})) establishes the general S-Score lower bound:

PS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)\displaystyle\mathrm{PS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}) ≥max⁡{0,P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a,𝐀−i=𝐜))−P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=𝐜))1−P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=𝐜))}\displaystyle\geq\max\left\{0,\,\frac{P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a,\,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}))-P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}))}{1-P(Y{=}1\mid do(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}))}\right\}

Thus

PS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)\displaystyle\mathrm{PS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}) ≥S(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜).\displaystyle\geq\mathrm{S}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}).

∎

A.3 Theoretical Properties

In this section, we discuss two key theoretical properties of our contribution metrics that directly underpin our experimental design and diagnostic analysis in the main text: (i) the exact identification of PN and PS under monotonicity versus our conservative lower bounds under LLM non-monotonicity, and (ii) the rationale for our asymmetric prerequisite control scheme over 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i}.

A.3.1 Exact Identification under Monotonicity

In the probabilities of causation framework [29, 38], when the monotonicity assumption holds, the Fréchet lower bounds in Theorems A.3 and A.4 tighten to exact equality.

Proposition A.5 (Exact Identification under Monotonicity; [38]).

Under the setting of Theorems A.3 and A.4, if YY is monotonic with respect to XiX_{i} across contrast (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}) under context 𝐜\mathbf{c} (i.e., P𝐜​(Ya=0,Ya′=1)=0P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}=0,Y_{a^{\prime}}=1)=0), then N-Score and S-Score equal PN and PS.

For the detailed proof, we refer the reader to Tian and Pearl [38]. In LLM evaluation, however, we do not impose the monotonicity assumption (Property 3.6), as we discussed in Section 3. Meanwhile, as our experiments in Section 5.2 show, injecting an incorrect answer (Ai=0A_{i}=0) can provide a reasoning scaffold that guides downstream deduction better than providing no information (Ai=∅A_{i}=\varnothing), causing RC​(Xi)\text{RC}(X_{i}) to exceed NC​(Xi)\text{NC}(X_{i}).

A.3.2 Remaining Prerequisite 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i} Controlling

Controlling for Remaining Prerequisites 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i}.

In a multi-parent SCM, the causal effect of a unit task XiX_{i} on the final outcome YY is also influenced by the states of the remaining prerequisites 𝐀−i:=𝐀Pa⁡(Y)∖{Xi}\mathbf{A}_{-i}{:=}\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(Y)\setminus\{X_{i}\}}. When 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i} is left un-intervened in the natural state ∅\varnothing, the actual realizations of these prerequisites remain unobserved and depend on each model’s upstream proficiency, which conflates XiX_{i}’s causal effect with model-specific upstream variations. To isolate XiX_{i}’s contribution under controlled conditions, our general definitions (Definitions A.1 and A.2) allow 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i} to take any intervention state configuration 𝐜∈𝒜|Pa⁡(Y)|−1\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{A}^{|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)|-1}. Because each prerequisite takes one of three states in 𝒜={1,0,∅}\mathcal{A}{=}\{1,0,\varnothing\}, the full configuration space contains 3|Pa⁡(Y)|−13^{|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)|-1} possible combinations. To evaluate XiX_{i} across representative prerequisite contexts without enumerating this exponential space, we restrict 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i} to homogeneous configurations where all remaining prerequisites share the same state c∈{1,0,∅}c\in\{1,0,\varnothing\}. This reduction yields three interpretable background environments: the oracle environment (𝐀−i=1\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}1), the corrupted environment (𝐀−i=0\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}0), and the natural environment (𝐀−i=∅\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\varnothing).

Asymmetric Prerequisite Control in N-Score and S-Score.

To capture complementary diagnostic properties across these homogeneous environments, our main-text definitions of N-Score and S-Score (Definitions 3.7 and 3.8) assign asymmetric background states to 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i} for any ordered contrast (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}). Specifically, N-Score sets 𝐀−i=a\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}a, whereas S-Score sets 𝐀−i=a′\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}a^{\prime}. This design aligns each metric with its intended diagnostic role in LLM evaluation. For N-Score, conditioning on 𝐀−i=a\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}a establishes a baseline environment where all prerequisites begin at state aa, allowing the metric to measure single-task vulnerability when XiX_{i} alone degrades to a′a^{\prime}. For S-Score, conditioning on 𝐀−i=a′\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}a^{\prime} establishes a baseline environment where all prerequisites begin at state a′a^{\prime}, allowing the metric to measure single-task recovery when XiX_{i} alone upgrades to aa. Furthermore, combining this asymmetric control with our ordered contrasts (1,0)(1,0), (1,∅)(1,\varnothing), (∅,0)(\varnothing,0), and (0,∅)(0,\varnothing) systematically covers all three homogeneous environments 𝐀−i∈{1,0,∅}\mathbf{A}_{-i}\in\{1,0,\varnothing\} and assigns each contrast a distinct operational meaning. For instance, under contrast (1,∅)(1,\varnothing), S(1,∅)\mathrm{S}_{(1,\varnothing)} evaluates how providing the correct answer for XiX_{i} alone improves overall task accuracy in the natural environment (𝐀−i=∅\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\varnothing), directly identifying high-leverage targets for single-task repair. Under the same contrast, N(1,∅)\mathrm{N}_{(1,\varnothing)} measures how leaving XiX_{i} unassisted reduces accuracy in the oracle environment (𝐀−i=1\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}1). Similarly, contrasts (1,0)(1,0), (∅,0)(\varnothing,0), and (0,∅)(0,\varnothing) quantify the impact of prerequisite corruption and structural scaffolding across oracle, natural, and corrupted environments.

Algebraic Coupling under Identical Prerequisite Control.

Under our general definitions of N-Score and S-Score (Definitions A.1 and A.2), when both metrics are evaluated under the same prerequisite configuration 𝐜∈𝒜|Pa⁡(Y)|−1\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{A}^{|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)|-1}, they share a common interventional background do⁡(𝐀−i=𝐜)\mathrm{do}(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}). Within this shared environment, necessity and sufficiency are algebraically coupled through the Probability of Necessity and Sufficiency (PNS\mathrm{PNS}) [29, 38].

Proposition A.6 (Algebraic Coupling under Identical Context).

For any prerequisite unit task Xi∈Pa⁡(Y)X_{i}\in\mathrm{Pa}(Y), any ordered contrast (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}) of distinct states in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and any fixed prerequisite configuration 𝐜∈𝒜|Pa⁡(Y)|−1\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{A}^{|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)|-1}, let pa|𝐜:=P⁡(Y=1∣do⁡(Ai=a,𝐀−i=𝐜))p_{a|\mathbf{c}}:=P(Y{=}1\mid\mathrm{do}(A_{i}{=}a,\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})) and pa′|𝐜:=P⁡(Y=1∣do⁡(Ai=a′,𝐀−i=𝐜))p_{a^{\prime}|\mathbf{c}}:=P(Y{=}1\mid\mathrm{do}(A_{i}{=}a^{\prime},\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})). Denote the conditional Probability of Necessity and Sufficiency under context 𝐜\mathbf{c} as PNS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜):=P⁡(Ya=1,Ya′=0∣do⁡(𝐀−i=𝐜))\mathrm{PNS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}):=P(Y_{a}{=}1,Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0\mid\mathrm{do}(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})). Under exogeneity assumption (Assumption 3.3), the exact counterfactual probabilities satisfy:

PN(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)⋅pa|𝐜=PS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)⋅(1−pa′|𝐜)=PNS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜),\small\mathrm{PN}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\cdot p_{a|\mathbf{c}}=\mathrm{PS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\cdot(1-p_{a^{\prime}|\mathbf{c}})=\mathrm{PNS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}), (11)

and the general N-Score and S-Score satisfy the parallel lower-bound coupling:

N(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)⋅pa|𝐜=S(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)⋅(1−pa′|𝐜)=max⁡{0,pa|𝐜−pa′|𝐜}≤PNS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜).\small\mathrm{N}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\cdot p_{a|\mathbf{c}}=\mathrm{S}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\cdot(1-p_{a^{\prime}|\mathbf{c}})=\max\big\{0,\;p_{a|\mathbf{c}}-p_{a^{\prime}|\mathbf{c}}\big\}\leq\mathrm{PNS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}). (12)
Proof.

Let P𝐜(⋅):=P(⋅∣do(𝐀−i=𝐜))P_{\mathbf{c}}(\cdot):=P(\cdot\mid\mathrm{do}(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c})) denote the probability measure in the submodel induced by do⁡(𝐀−i=𝐜)\mathrm{do}(\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}\mathbf{c}) [28]. Under exogeneity ssumption, conditioning on AiA_{i} within this submodel is operationally identical to intervening on it, so P𝐜​(Ya=1)=pa|𝐜P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1)=p_{a|\mathbf{c}} and P𝐜​(Ya′=0)=1−pa′|𝐜P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0)=1-p_{a^{\prime}|\mathbf{c}}. By consistency and the definition of conditional probability, PN(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)⋅pa|𝐜=P𝐜​(Ya′=0∣Ai=a,Y=1)⋅P𝐜​(Y=1∣Ai=a)=P𝐜​(Ya=1,Ya′=0)=PNS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)\mathrm{PN}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\cdot p_{a|\mathbf{c}}=P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0\mid A_{i}{=}a,Y{=}1)\cdot P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y{=}1\mid A_{i}{=}a)=P_{\mathbf{c}}(Y_{a}{=}1,Y_{a^{\prime}}{=}0)=\mathrm{PNS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}). An analogous expansion yields PS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)⋅(1−pa′|𝐜)=PNS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)\mathrm{PS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\cdot(1-p_{a^{\prime}|\mathbf{c}})=\mathrm{PNS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c}), establishing Equation (11).

Next, multiplying Definition A.1 by pa|𝐜p_{a|\mathbf{c}} and Definition A.2 by 1−pa′|𝐜1-p_{a^{\prime}|\mathbf{c}} directly gives max⁡{0,pa|𝐜−pa′|𝐜}\max\{0,p_{a|\mathbf{c}}-p_{a^{\prime}|\mathbf{c}}\}. Applying the classical Fréchet inequality yields PNS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣𝐜)≥max⁡{0,pa|𝐜+(1−pa′|𝐜)−1}=max⁡{0,pa|𝐜−pa′|𝐜}\mathrm{PNS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid\mathbf{c})\geq\max\{0,p_{a|\mathbf{c}}+(1-p_{a^{\prime}|\mathbf{c}})-1\}=\max\{0,p_{a|\mathbf{c}}-p_{a^{\prime}|\mathbf{c}}\}, which establishes Equation 12. ∎

Metric Independence under Asymmetric Control.

Proposition A.6 shows that necessity and sufficiency are algebraically convertible when evaluated within the same background environment 𝐜\mathbf{c}. However, note that in our main-text formulation (Definitions 3.7 and 3.8), N-Score and S-Score evaluate XiX_{i} across two distinct background environments: N-Score conditions on 𝐀−i=a\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}a, whereas S-Score conditions on 𝐀−i=a′\mathbf{A}_{-i}{=}a^{\prime}. Whenever YY depends on multiple prerequisites (|Pa⁡(Y)|>1|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)|>1), the contrast states a≠a′a\neq a^{\prime} place the remaining prerequisites into two different interventional configurations. Because the two metrics operate under distinct prerequisite states, their numerators correspond to the Fréchet lower bounds of two different conditional PNS\mathrm{PNS} quantities, PNS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣a)\mathrm{PNS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid a) and PNS(a,a′)​(Xi,Y∣a′)\mathrm{PNS}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{i},Y\mid a^{\prime}), where in general pa|a−pa′|a≠pa|a′−pa′|a′p_{a|a}-p_{a^{\prime}|a}\neq p_{a|a^{\prime}}-p_{a^{\prime}|a^{\prime}}. Consequently, our main-text N-Score and S-Score cannot be algebraically derived from one another through marginal outcome probabilities. A special case arises when |Pa⁡(Y)|=1|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)|{=}1, representing the single-parent setting where 𝐀−i\mathbf{A}_{-i} is empty; in this case, both metrics operate within the same unconditional environment and reduce directly to the classical coupled relationship in Equation 12. For general multi-parent tasks, this LLM-specific decoupling ensures that N-Score and S-Score serve as independent diagnostic dimensions, allowing each paired (a,a′)(a,a^{\prime}) score to provide distinct and practical diagnostic value for pinpointing failure bottlenecks versus high-leverage repair targets.

A.4 Markov Chain Structure

In Section 4, we introduced Markov chain unit tasks to represent sub-problems that require iterative solving across sequential steps. In the task-level SCM (Figure 2), a Markov chain unit task is represented as a single composite node that receives inputs from upstream prerequisites and feeds into downstream tasks. To analyze how model capabilities and error propagation evolve over long reasoning horizons, we unfold this composite node into an explicit sequential chain of unit tasks (Section 5.4). Below, we formalize the Markov chain structure within a task decomposition SCM and derive its step-wise causal properties.

Definition A.7 (Markov Chain Structure in Task Decomposition SCM).

Consider a task decomposition SCM (Definition 3.1). A Markov chain structure is a recursive sub-model region defined over TT sequential reasoning steps (t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T), where each step consists of a recurring cycle of pp constituent unit tasks (p≥1p\geq 1), represented by unit task variables X1(t),X2(t),…,Xp(t)X_{1}^{(t)},X_{2}^{(t)},\dots,X_{p}^{(t)}. Each unit task variable Xi(t)X_{i}^{(t)} is given by the structural assignment:

Xi(t):=fi(t)(Pa(Xi(t)),Ni(t)),for i=1,…,p,t=1,…,T,X_{i}^{(t)}:=f_{i}^{(t)}\Big(\mathrm{Pa}\big(X_{i}^{(t)}\big),\;N_{i}^{(t)}\Big),\quad\text{for }i=1,\dots,p,\;\;t=1,\dots,T, (13)

where fi(t)f_{i}^{(t)} is the structural function determining Xi(t)X_{i}^{(t)}, Ni(t)N_{i}^{(t)} is the exogenous noise variable, and the parent set Pa⁡(Xi(t))\mathrm{Pa}\big(X_{i}^{(t)}\big) is uniquely defined by:

Pa⁡(Xi(t))={{Xi−1(t)},if ​i∈{2,…,p},{Xp(t−1)},if ​i=1​ and ​t∈{2,…,T},\mathrm{Pa}\big(X_{i}^{(t)}\big)=\begin{cases}\big\{X_{i-1}^{(t)}\big\},&\text{if }i\in\{2,\dots,p\},\\[4.0pt] \big\{X_{p}^{(t-1)}\big\},&\text{if }i=1\text{ and }t\in\{2,\dots,T\},\end{cases} (14)

with the initial prerequisite set Pa⁡(X1(1))\mathrm{Pa}\big(X_{1}^{(1)}\big) given by the upstream prerequisites external to the Markov chain region in the SCM (or ∅\emptyset if the chain originates at a root node). Unfolding this recursive dependency across all TT steps yields the explicit sequential causal chain:

X1(1)→X2(1)→⋯→Xp(1)→X1(2)→⋯→Xp(T−1)→X1(T)→⋯→Xp(T).\small X_{1}^{(1)}\to X_{2}^{(1)}\to\cdots\to X_{p}^{(1)}\;\to\;X_{1}^{(2)}\to\cdots\to X_{p}^{(T-1)}\;\to\;X_{1}^{(T)}\to\cdots\to X_{p}^{(T)}. (15)
Remark A.8.

In the unfolded Markov chain structure (Definition A.7), every non-initial unit task variable XjX_{j} has a single causal prerequisite, i.e., |Pa⁡(Xj)|=1|\mathrm{Pa}(X_{j})|=1. Consequently, for any such unit task XjX_{j} and its unique direct parent Xprev∈Pa⁡(Xj)X_{\mathrm{prev}}\in\mathrm{Pa}(X_{j}), the set of remaining prerequisites is empty:

𝐀−prev:=𝐀Pa⁡(Xj)∖{Xprev}=∅.\mathbf{A}_{-\mathrm{prev}}:=\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{Pa}(X_{j})\setminus\{X_{\mathrm{prev}}\}}=\emptyset. (16)

Under this single-parent setting, 𝐜∈𝒜|Pa⁡(Xj)∖{Xprev}|\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{A}^{|\mathrm{Pa}(X_{j})\setminus\{X_{\mathrm{prev}}\}|} in Definitions A.1 and A.2 becomes ∅\emptyset, and the N-Score and S-Score simplify to:

N(a,a′)​(Xprev,Xj)\displaystyle\mathrm{N}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{\mathrm{prev}},X_{j}) =max⁡{0,P⁡(Xj=1∣d​o​(Aprev=a))−P⁡(Xj=1∣d​o​(Aprev=a′))P⁡(Xj=1∣d​o​(Aprev=a))},\displaystyle=\max\left\{0,\;\frac{P\big(X_{j}=1\mid do(A_{\mathrm{prev}}=a)\big)-P\big(X_{j}=1\mid do(A_{\mathrm{prev}}=a^{\prime})\big)}{P\big(X_{j}=1\mid do(A_{\mathrm{prev}}=a)\big)}\right\}, (17)
S(a,a′)​(Xprev,Xj)\displaystyle\mathrm{S}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{\mathrm{prev}},X_{j}) =max⁡{0,P⁡(Xj=1∣d​o​(Aprev=a))−P⁡(Xj=1∣d​o​(Aprev=a′))1−P⁡(Xj=1∣d​o​(Aprev=a′))}.\displaystyle=\max\left\{0,\;\frac{P\big(X_{j}=1\mid do(A_{\mathrm{prev}}=a)\big)-P\big(X_{j}=1\mid do(A_{\mathrm{prev}}=a^{\prime})\big)}{1-P\big(X_{j}=1\mid do(A_{\mathrm{prev}}=a^{\prime})\big)}\right\}.

As an immediate consequence, Proposition A.6 directly holds without requiring external context conditioning:

N(a,a′)​(Xprev,Xj)⋅pa\displaystyle\mathrm{N}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{\mathrm{prev}},X_{j})\cdot p_{a} =S(a,a′)​(Xprev,Xj)⋅(1−pa′)=max⁡{0,pa−pa′},\displaystyle=\mathrm{S}_{(a,a^{\prime})}(X_{\mathrm{prev}},X_{j})\cdot(1-p_{a^{\prime}})=\max\{0,\;p_{a}-p_{a^{\prime}}\}, (18)

where pa=P⁡(Xj=1∣d​o​(Aprev=a))p_{a}=P\big(X_{j}=1\mid do(A_{\mathrm{prev}}=a)\big), pa′=P⁡(Xj=1∣d​o​(Aprev=a′)CLOSEp_{a^{\prime}}=P\big(X_{j}=1\mid do(A_{\mathrm{prev}}=a^{\prime}), and max⁡{0,pa−pa′}\max\{0,\;p_{a}-p_{a^{\prime}}\} is the N​SNS score reported in Sec. 5.4, denoting lower bound of PNS.

In our CADET benchmark, three tasks contain Markov chain structures with cycle lengths p=1p=1 (Maze, Map Navigation) and p=2p=2 (Multistep vision reasoning) (Figure 2), corresponding to the step-wise evaluations in Sec. 5.4 (Figure 10).

Appendix B Details of Benchmark

B.1 Benchmark Composition

B.1.1 Task Inventory and Statistics

This section reports the benchmark details following our Section 4. Table 2 lists the 10 overall evaluation tasks, and Table 3 reports the overview and structure of their task-level SCMs, reported depth is the length of the longest directed path terminating at YY.

B.1.2 Capability Categories

We group unit tasks into four categories according to the kind of information the task requires the model to produce. Each unit task is assigned to the category of the capability it primarily targets.

  • •

    Perception: reading out the presence, identity, category, or image position of an object from the visual signal, without relating separate elements to one another.

  • •

    Spatial: relating elements to each other or to the observer, covering distance, size, orientation, viewpoint, and navigation.

  • •

    Temporal: relating observations across frames or views, covering motion, ordering, and localization in time.

  • •

    Cognitive: operating on already extracted facts, covering counting, arithmetic, causal attribution, and multi-step or goal-directed reasoning.

The overall task of each SCM is labelled with the same four categories (Table 2). Across the 46 unit tasks, the four categories contain 15, 12, 10, and 9 tasks respectively.

B.1.3 Per-Task SCM and Unit Task

Table 4 specifies the unit tasks and SCM structure of every evaluation task, giving for each node its capability, category, answer format, number of questions, and parent set. Nodes are indexed in a topological order of the task-level SCM. As a result, CADET contains over 33,000 unit task level questions.

B.2 Benchmark Design Rationale

Task Selection. The 10 evaluation tasks in CADET are selected based on three considerations. First, we focus on problems where current frontier MLLMs remain far from saturated under end-to-end evaluation, so that the diagnosis concerns capability gaps that current models still struggle with. Second, we select compositional tasks that require multiple interdependent capabilities to reach the final answer, so that each task admits a meaningful decomposition into unit tasks. Third, we prioritize real-world visual scenarios across single-image, multi-image, and video modalities, and the resulting 46 unit tasks cover perception, spatial, temporal, and cognitive capabilities.

Prerequisite Identification and SCM Structure. Each unit task corresponds to a single capability. A capability is included in the decomposition of an evaluation task when it is a required information for answering the overall task question. For example, to tell the number on the top face of a dice, one needs to know where the dice is and which face is its top face; to tell the direction of a pedestrian relative to the ego vehicle, one needs to locate the pedestrian and determine the viewpoint of the camera that observes it. We specify a prerequisite dependency from XjX_{j} to XiX_{i} when solving XiX_{i} requires the information or the capability represented by XjX_{j}. The same task structure is used for all evaluated models. We discuss the completeness of the specified SCMs in Appendix E.

Unit-Task Question Granularity. As shown in Tables 2 and 4, the number of questions of a unit task is not necessarily equal to the number of overall task instances. When an overall task is built on multiple images, video frames, or target objects, the capability of a unit task does not necessarily apply at the same granularity, and querying all of them within a single bundled question would turn the unit task into a multi-target aggregation problem. In such cases, we formulate separate questions at the granularity at which the capability applies. For example, when a task instance contains five images, object identification is asked separately for each image; when a task instance contains several target objects, object localization is asked separately for each object.

B.3 Benchmark Construction

B.3.1 Image/Video Source and License

As described in Section 4, while all evaluation questions, task decompositions, and unit-task annotations in CADET are newly created to mitigate data contamination, the underlying source images and videos are curated from publicly available datasets and open repositories with permissive licenses. Table 5 summarizes all source media (image and video) used in CADET, along with their corresponding descriptions, references, and license terms.

B.3.2 Data Construction and Quality Assurance

Two-Stage Construction and Closed-Form Annotation. We construct CADET in two stages following predefined task structures. In the first stage, for each of the 10 overall tasks, we define the task scope, a question-answer template, and detailed task instructions on the selected source images and videos. Raters follow these instructions and templates to write the overall task question and its ground-truth answer. In the second stage, to decompose each overall task into unit tasks without introducing noise from free-form question writing, we design the decomposition step as closed-form annotation and labeling tasks. Depending on the unit task, raters draw bounding boxes or paths on the images and provide labels that follow strict format specifications. Once these annotations are collected, we extract the labeled information and convert it into unit-task questions, correct answers (Ai=1A_{i}=1), and rendered visual annotations through structured templates. For the incorrect answers (Ai=0A_{i}=0), structured unit tasks use random sampling over plausible candidates; specifically, for numerical tasks, we sample within a bounded local neighborhood around the ground truth (e.g., within ±2\pm 2 of a groundtruth value of 55) rather than drawing distant values (e.g., 2020) that models would trivially rule out. For the remaining three free-form text tasks where random sampling is not applicable, raters write the incorrect answers following instructions designed to minimize subjective bias.

Two-Rater Iterative Verification. All annotations are conducted by a pool of over 130 experienced multimodal raters. Across both stages, every instance is processed by two raters in sequence: the first rater completes the annotation, and a second quality-check rater independently inspects the result. If the quality-check rater identifies an inaccurate answer, an imprecise bounding box or path, or a label that violates the required format specification, the instance is returned to the first rater for revision. This review cycle repeats until the quality-check rater accepts the annotation.

Instance Revision and Corner-Case Filtering. At every annotation step, raters can flag issues with a candidate instance. When a question requires minor rephrasing or an answer can be refined against clear visual content, raters directly update the item within the review loop; when an instance cannot be resolved or cleanly annotated at the unit-task level, raters are instructed to drop it. Beyond ambiguities in the overall task, drops in the second stage occur when an intermediate unit task cannot be reliably annotated across frames or views. Typical cases include a spatial reference (such as a roadside curb) shifting to the image boundary with insufficient visibility, a target vehicle tracked across views becoming too small or partially occluded in a later frame, or a second vehicle of the same color partially entering the scene and preventing unique target identification. Removing such instances ensures that every unit task in the SCM admits a well-defined intervention state. Across 1,467 candidate instances dispatched for annotation, 323 (22.0%) were dropped under these criteria, yielding the final 1,144 instances and over 33,000 unit-task questions in CADET.

Appendix C Experiments Setup

Evaluated Models. We evaluate 12 MLLMs across six model families: Gemini 3.1 Pro [12], Gemini 3.5 Flash [15], Gemini 3 Flash [10], Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite [11], GPT-5.4 [27], GPT-5.4 Nano [27], Grok 4.3 [45], Gemma 4 31B [6], Gemma 4 26B [6], Qwen3.5-397B-A17B [32], Qwen3.6 27B [33], and Kimi K2.5 [37]. The Gemini, GPT, Grok and Gemma models are queried through the official APIs, while the remaining open-weight models are queried via OpenRouter. All models are run with their default sampling settings, maximum supported output tokens, and thinking mode set to high (or left at the default active setting when not configurable).

LLM-as-a-judge details. Among the 46 unit tasks, 43 use structured output formats (multiple-choice, integer, or coordinate) and are evaluated via deterministic rule-based parsing and exact match, while the remaining 3 free-form text unit tasks are evaluated using Gemini 3.6 Flash [16] by comparing model predictions against ground-truth reference answers. Although these 3 unit tasks do not constrain outputs to option letters or numbers, each still pairs with a concise, specific reference answer (e.g., an atomic action such as “turn left”), so the judge only checks whether the predicted phrase conveys the same meaning as the reference. For the 43 structured unit tasks, Gemini 3.6 Flash is invoked strictly as a fallback when a response deviates from the required surface format (e.g., outputting “So the answer is **C**.” instead of “C”). Across all evaluation runs on structured unit tasks, deterministic exact match directly resolves 98.03%98.03\% of predictions, with only 1.97%1.97\% triggering the LLM-as-a-judge fallback.

Prompts. Figures 11 and 12 present the prompt templates used to assemble intervened prerequisite context and to run the LLM judge, respectively. For active interventions (Ai∈{1,0}A_{i}\in\{1,0\}), the prerequisites Pa​(Xi)\text{Pa}(X_{i}) are formatted as a structured JSON question–answer block and prepended to the target task query using the same template for both Ai=1A_{i}=1 and Ai=0A_{i}=0, differing only in the filled prerequisite answer values (along with the corresponding visual annotations rendered on the image when Ai=1A_{i}=1 represents spatial ground truth). Under the natural state (Ai=∅A_{i}=\varnothing), the prerequisite context block is omitted while the target question and output-format instructions remain the same.

Appendix D More Experiment Results

D.1 More Capability Diagnosis Results (NC, IC, RC)

This section provides additional visualizations and the complete numerical results supporting the capability diagnostics in Section 5.2. First, whereas Section 5.2 focuses on the 30 non-root unit tasks (Pa​(Xi)≠∅\text{Pa}(X_{i})\neq\emptyset) that admit upstream interventions, Figure 13,14 and Table 7,6 incorporate the 16 foundational root unit tasks (Pa​(Xi)=∅\text{Pa}(X_{i})=\emptyset, for which only natural capability NC is defined), comparing root NC against non-root NC and IC across individual models (Figure 14, Table 7) and capability categories (Figure. 13, Table 6). Second, Figure 15,16 and Table 8,9 expand the compact RC−NC\text{RC}-\text{NC} summary in Figure 4 of the main text by plotting absolute NC and RC levels alongside their signed differences at the category level (Figure 15, Table 8) and across all 12 models within each category (Figure 16, Table 9), reporting the full per-group means and standard deviations.

Comparing Non-Root Capabilities (NC, IC) with Foundational Root Capabilities (NC). Because root unit tasks have no modeled upstream prerequisites in the task SCM (Pa​(Xi)=∅\text{Pa}(X_{i})=\emptyset), their natural capability (NC) assesses foundational proficiency independently of upstream prerequisite states. Under unassisted evaluation (do​(𝐀Pa​(Xi)=∅)\text{do}(\mathbf{A}_{\text{Pa}(X_{i})}=\emptyset)), models achieve higher accuracy on the 16 root unit tasks than on the 30 downstream non-root unit tasks: as reported in Table 7 and Figure 14, mean NC across the 12 models is 0.7400.740 on root nodes versus 0.4900.490 on non-root nodes (a difference of +0.250+0.250, ranging from +0.169+0.169 to +0.301+0.301 across individual models). A consistent NC difference between root and non-root nodes appears within each category that contains root tasks (Table 6, Figure 13): Perception (0.7750.775 vs. 0.5900.590), Spatial (0.6270.627 vs. 0.5560.556), and Temporal (0.7140.714 vs. 0.4600.460), while Cognitive unit tasks occur exclusively as non-root nodes (Pa​(Xi)≠∅\text{Pa}(X_{i})\neq\emptyset) and score lowest under unassisted evaluation (NC=0.406\text{NC}=0.406). When correct prerequisite answers are supplied (do​(𝐀Pa​(Xi)=1)\text{do}(\mathbf{A}_{\text{Pa}(X_{i})}=1)), mean non-root IC across models rises to 0.6880.688 against the 0.7400.740 root NC baseline (narrowing the overall gap from 0.2500.250 to 0.0520.052, with differences as small as −0.010-0.010 for GPT-5.4 and 0.0020.002 for GPT-5.4n). Across categories, this comparison reinforces the capability profile in Section 5.2: Perception maintains high accuracy on both root tasks (NC=0.775\text{NC}=0.775) and prerequisite-supplied non-root tasks (IC=0.796\text{IC}=0.796), and Cognitive non-root tasks rise from NC=0.406\text{NC}=0.406 to IC=0.721\text{IC}=0.721, approaching the average root-node baseline (0.7400.740). By contrast, Spatial exhibits the lowest root-node accuracy (NC=0.627\text{NC}=0.627) and reaches a similarly bounded ceiling on non-root tasks when prerequisites are supplied (IC=0.671\text{IC}=0.671), while Temporal non-root tasks reach IC=0.614\text{IC}=0.614 (vs. 0.7140.714 on root tasks), consistent with the persistent residual gaps (1−IC1-\text{IC}) in spatial and temporal capabilities identified in the main text.

Expanded Breakdown of Resilience Capability (RC vs. NC). Figure 15 and Table 8 complement Figure 4 by displaying NC and RC on the same absolute capability scale across categories, while Figure 16 and Table 9 provide the disaggregated per-model profiles parallel to Figure 3(b–e). On average across the 12 models (Table 8), injecting incorrect prerequisite answers (do​(𝐀Pa​(Xi)=0)\text{do}(\mathbf{A}_{\text{Pa}(X_{i})}=0)) yields lower accuracy than unassisted evaluation in Perception (0.590→0.4460.590\to 0.446, RC−NC=−0.144\text{RC}-\text{NC}=-0.144), Spatial (0.556→0.4390.556\to 0.439, −0.116-0.116), and Temporal (0.460→0.4140.460\to 0.414, −0.046-0.046), corresponding to an overall non-root difference of −0.054-0.054 (0.490→0.4350.490\to 0.435), whereas Cognitive tasks exhibit a modest positive shift (0.406→0.4450.406\to 0.445, +0.040+0.040). The per-model breakdown in Figure 16 and Table 9 shows that these category-level trends hold consistently across model families and scales: all 12 models exhibit RC<NC\text{RC}<\text{NC} in Perception and Spatial, 11 of 12 decline in Temporal (with GPT-5.4n showing a +0.030+0.030 shift), and 10 of 12 show positive RC−NC\text{RC}-\text{NC} shifts in Cognitive (all except GPT-5.4 at −0.018-0.018 and Kimi K2.5 at −0.066-0.066), providing the full per-model evidence for the non-monotonicity discussed in Property 3.6 and Section 5.2.

D.2 More Causal Contribution Diagnosis Results (NN, SS-Score)

In this section, we provide additional experimental results complementing the causal contribution analysis in Section 5.3. Figure 17 reports prerequisite NN- and SS-Scores under the remaining three state contrasts (1,0)(1,0), (0,∅)(0,\varnothing), and (∅,0)(\varnothing,0) (complementing (1,∅)(1,\varnothing) in Figure 5). Figure 18 disaggregates these three contrasts by task pattern and model group (extending Figure 6). Figure 19 shows the inter-model rank agreement across all eight contribution scores, and Figure 20 provides the per-prerequisite breakdown across the four state contrasts. To prevent small denominators from producing numerically unstable ratios in Eqs. (5)–(6), we set a score to 00 whenever its baseline denominator falls below 0.100.10. Crucially, this threshold has zero effect on six of the eight metrics and affects only 3.0%3.0\% (94/3,16894/3{,}168) of all scores, concentrated in N⁡(0,∅)N(0,\varnothing) (with a small remainder in N⁡(∅,0)N(\varnothing,0)). This is expected by design: N⁡(0,∅)N(0,\varnothing) measures the success drop from setting a prerequisite to ∅\varnothing in the all-incorrect (00) environment, where baseline success RC⁡(Y)\mathrm{RC}(Y) is naturally near zero whenever incorrect prerequisites prevent task completion.

Corrupting a prerequisite reduces success more than leaving it unassisted. N⁡(1,0)N(1,0) and N⁡(1,∅)N(1,\varnothing) share the same oracle baseline where all prerequisites are correctly provided, differing only in whether XiX_{i} receives an incorrect answer or is left unassisted. Across prerequisites, N⁡(1,0)N(1,0) consistently exceeds N⁡(1,∅)N(1,\varnothing) (Figure 17a vs. Figure 5), shifting more prerequisites into the high-NN / low-SS quadrant and fewer into the low-NN / high-SS quadrant. For example, on the perception prerequisites of Music Note, N⁡(1,∅)N(1,\varnothing) is low (0.040.04–0.160.16) and S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) is high (0.510.51–0.590.59): omitting a single prerequisite in the oracle setting incurs minimal loss, while supplying it alone in the natural state recovers over half of the failures. Under (1,0)(1,0), however, N⁡(1,0)N(1,0) rises to 0.270.27–0.730.73 and S⁡(1,0)S(1,0) falls to at most 0.020.02: a single incorrect prerequisite removes a substantial fraction of oracle success, while correcting one prerequisite when others remain incorrect recovers almost no failures. Similarly, under (∅,0)(\varnothing,0) (Figure 17c), prerequisites shift along N⁡(∅,0)N(\varnothing,0) into the high-NN / low-SS region, whereas under (0,∅)(0,\varnothing) (Figure 17b), most prerequisites remain near zero with positive values concentrated in specific prerequisites examined in Figure 20.

Separation between SOTA and Others under prerequisite corruption. When disaggregated by task pattern and model group (Figure 18), SOTA and Others separate clearly in Pattern 2 across all three contrasts involving incorrect prerequisites: S⁡(1,0)S(1,0), S⁡(∅,0)S(\varnothing,0), and N⁡(1,0)N(1,0) (Figure 18c,d,k,l). Starting from the all-incorrect environment, SOTA achieves consistently higher single-prerequisite recovery than Others both when correcting a single prerequisite (S⁡(1,0)S(1,0): 0.1430.143–0.2630.263 for SOTA vs. 0.0290.029–0.1050.105 for Others) and when removing a single incorrect answer (S⁡(∅,0)S(\varnothing,0): 0.0440.044–0.1520.152 vs. 0.0150.015–0.0280.028). Symmetrically, starting from the oracle environment, corrupting a single prerequisite causes smaller drops for SOTA (N⁡(1,0)N(1,0): 0.0970.097–0.1060.106) than for Others (0.1080.108–0.2950.295), mirroring the shift toward higher NN and lower SS for Others under (1,∅)(1,\varnothing) in Figure 6.

Inter-model agreement on high-S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) prerequisites. Among the eight contribution metrics, S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) exhibits the strongest inter-model agreement, with a mean pairwise Spearman correlation of 0.720.72, compared with 0.410.41 for N⁡(1,∅)N(1,\varnothing) (Figure 19). Thus, the high-leverage prerequisites that recover natural failures when supplied alone are largely shared across models, whereas sensitivity to single-prerequisite omission in the oracle setting varies more across models. Agreement on S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) is especially strong among the four SOTA models (mean ρ=0.85\rho=0.85 vs. 0.700.70 among Others), holding both within the Gemini series (0.870.87) and across families between GPT-5.4 and Gemini (0.840.84), and within individual tasks the top-S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) prerequisite is identical or shared between the same top pair across models on the majority of tasks.

Cross-contrast consistency and per-prerequisite breakdown. Across prerequisites, rankings correlate positively between N⁡(1,∅)N(1,\varnothing) and N⁡(1,0)N(1,0) (Spearman ρ=0.64\rho=0.64) and between S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) and S⁡(1,0)S(1,0) (ρ=0.53\rho=0.53; Figure 20), indicating that prerequisites whose omission most reduces oracle performance also tend to be the most destructive when corrupted, and those that best recover natural failures also drive recovery in the all-incorrect setting. For transitions between ∅\varnothing and 00, (∅,0)(\varnothing,0) and (0,∅)(0,\varnothing) measure opposite directions of the same state pair; under zero-clipping, at most one direction is active for a given model and prerequisite, separating performance degradation from incorrect prerequisites (N⁡(∅,0),S⁡(∅,0)N(\varnothing,0),S(\varnothing,0)) from positive recovery when an incorrect prerequisite is provided over no prerequisite (S⁡(0,∅),N⁡(0,∅)S(0,\varnothing),N(0,\varnothing)) under Property 3.6. Consistent with Section 5.2 and Figure 9, positive S⁡(0,∅)S(0,\varnothing) values appear primarily on prerequisites feeding into downstream cognitive or spatial-relational integration—such as Temporal Sequencing (0.340.34), Temporal Localization (0.110.11), and Object Localization (0.070.07) in Traffic Causation, and Viewpoint Estimation (0.230.23) in Surround Loc.—while remaining near zero on foundational perception and spatial prerequisites.

D.3 Detail Explanation of Markov Chain Unit Task Results

Section 5.4 analyzes the three Markov chain unit tasks in CADET (Figure 10): Maze and Multistep Reasoning, whose primary task structure is a Markov chain, together with the route-planning unit task embedded within Map Navigation. While all three share the same Markov sequential dependency structure (Definition A.7), they differ in their concrete step-wise logic, and because this distinction directly manifests in their empirical behavior, we group them into the two regimes discussed in Section 5.4: goal-directed and process-cumulative. In Maze, the trajectory from the start to the exit is partitioned into T=10T{=}10 steps; because the overall query (identifying which candidate is the exit) cannot be further decomposed into distinct sub-questions, at each step tt the model is positioned at the tt-th waypoint to answer this same exit-identification question. Similarly, in the Markov chain node of Map Navigation, the model stands at each intermediate step along the route and looks toward a given destination to decide the next move. Both tasks are therefore goal-directed: conditioned on the current step tt, solving the task depends only on the remaining path toward the goal rather than the history already traversed. By contrast, Multistep Reasoning is process-cumulative: starting from an initial state without a pre-specified destination, the model follows movement rules where each step alternates between identifying the current Position and determining the current Action. Because the terminal state is unknown in advance, accurately resolving either node at step tt requires tracking the cumulative execution process from the starting point up to step tt.

To operationalize the ternary intervention at step tt along an unfolded chain, we provide the full preceding trajectory context from step 11 to t−1t{-}1 in the prompt. Under A=1A{=}1, we inject the ground-truth questions, answers, and corresponding visual annotations for all preceding steps. A special case arises in Maze: because every step asks the same exit-identification question and shares the identical ground-truth answer, injecting the textual answer of any preceding step would directly reveal the answer at step tt. For A=1A{=}1 in Maze, we therefore inject the preceding step questions without their textual answers, accompanied by the visual annotation on the image marking the current waypoint and the human-annotated path from the start up to step t−1t{-}1. Under A=0A{=}0, each preceding step from 11 to t−1t{-}1 is independently assigned a randomly sampled incorrect answer from the valid answer space via text only (Section 5.1), while A=∅A{=}\varnothing leaves the preceding trajectory unassisted.

D.4 Additional Experiments and Findings

D.4.1 Ablation on Intervention Modality

In the main experiments, the correct intervention (Ai=1A_{i}=1) injects both a textual answer and, where applicable, visual annotations (e.g., bounding boxes, trajectories) onto the image. To examine the role of visual annotations in this intervention, we also evaluate a text-answer-only condition Ai=1tA_{i}=1_{t}, which provides the same textual answer as Ai=1A_{i}=1 but keeps the original image unmodified. We run this condition on two models, Gemini 3.5 Flash from the top-4 (SOTA) group and Gemma-4-31B from the remaining (Others) group, across all 30 non-root unit tasks.

Figure 22(a) shows that 1t1_{t} closely approaches IC across all four capability categories. In temporal, the two conditions are virtually identical (both 0.66); in perception and spatial, they differ by only 0.02 (0.84 vs. 0.86; 0.70 vs. 0.72). The largest gap appears in cognitive (0.71 vs. 0.77), where 1t1_{t} nonetheless remains far above NC (0.44) and RC (0.47). Overall, 1t1_{t} reaches 0.71 against an IC of 0.74. The per-model results (Figure 22(b–e)) are consistent: for both models, 1t1_{t} tracks IC in every category, with a gap of at most 0.06 in any model–category pair. These results indicate that the textual answer accounts for the large majority of the capability gain under correct prerequisites, while the remaining difference between 1t1_{t} and IC reflects the additional contribution of visual annotations.

The same pattern holds for the causal contribution metrics. Figure 22 compares S⁡(1t,∅)S(1_{t},\varnothing) with 1t1_{t} in place of state 11, against S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) for each prerequisite. Spatial, temporal, and cognitive prerequisites lie along the diagonal, indicating that the magnitude and ranking of S-Scores are largely preserved without visual annotations. The systematic departures below the diagonal correspond to perception prerequisites, whose S⁡(1t,∅)S(1_{t},\varnothing) falls well below S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing). The corresponding N-Score comparison shows a similar agreement (Pearson r=0.87r=0.87 between N⁡(1t,∅)N(1_{t},\varnothing) and N⁡(1,∅)N(1,\varnothing) across all prerequisites).

D.4.2 Ablation on Question-Only Injection

In Section 5.2, incorrect prerequisites improve cognitive tasks for most models (RC >> NC), and in Section 5.3, S⁡(0,∅)S(0,\varnothing) is nonzero for some prerequisite categories, indicating that even incorrect answers occasionally help. Since the incorrect intervention (Ai=0A_{i}=0) injects both a sub-question and an incorrect answer, a natural follow-up is to ask how much of the prerequisite effect comes from the sub-question itself. We therefore evaluate a question-only condition Ai=qA_{i}=q, which injects each prerequisite’s sub-question without any answer, on the same two models. As shown in Figure 22(a), qq yields a modest improvement over NC (overall 0.58 vs. 0.53) but remains far below 1t1_{t} (0.71) and IC (0.74). Across categories, qq exceeds NC by at most 0.06, whereas 1t1_{t} exceeds NC by 0.09 (spatial) to 0.26 (cognitive). The causal contribution metrics show the same trend: S⁡(q,∅)S(q,\varnothing) averages 0.05 across prerequisites, compared with 0.26 for S⁡(1,∅)S(1,\varnothing) on the same two models, and S⁡(q,∅)S(q,\varnothing) does not exceed 0.09 in any prerequisite category. Thus, providing the sub-question without answer does improve performance, meanwhile the improvement is limited and remains far smaller than that from providing its answer.

Appendix E Discussion

On the Scope and Completeness of Task Decompositions.

The SCM of each task declares, for every target task, which unit tasks are placed under controlled intervention. It is not intended as an exhaustive characterization of the task’s causal structure or of the model’s internal computation, and we do not claim that it is complete: the set of factors that may influence a model’s answer on a real-world task is open-ended. A unit task is declared as a prerequisite of a target when solving the target requires the information it represents (Appendix. B.2), and the same declared structure is used for all evaluated models. Any factor outside the declared parent sets belongs to the unmodeled factors captured by NiN_{i} (Definition 3.1); it is not separately intervened on and remains in its natural regime.

Completeness is not required for the validity of the metrics. Every quantity entering the capability and contribution metrics is an interventional probability, estimated by directly running the model under the corresponding regime, including the natural regime ∅\varnothing, rather than inferred from co-occurrences between unit-task outcomes. The lower-bound guarantees (Theorems A.3 and A.4) hold for any configuration 𝐜\mathbf{c} of the remaining declared prerequisites and rest on prerequisite regimes being assigned through injection (Assumption 3.3), not on the declared parent sets capturing every factor that influences the outcome. N- and S-Scores therefore remain valid lower bounds on PN and PS for the context actually realized, in which the target’s declared prerequisites are set as specified and all other factors are left in their natural regime.

What the decomposition determines is the reference set against which each metric is read (Section 3.3): IC measures performance on XiX_{i} when its declared prerequisites are supplied correctly, IC−NC\text{IC}-\text{NC} is the net gain from supplying them (the cascading component in Section 5.2), and 1−IC1-\text{IC} is the residual error that persists under correct prerequisites. The category-level findings in Section 5.2 are statements of this form, namely which share of the natural error is resolved by supplying the declared prerequisites and which share persists, obtained under the same inclusion criterion for every category.

Finally, declared dependencies are task-defined, whereas the extent to which a model relies on each of them is measured rather than assumed. Averaged within each category, supplying the declared prerequisites improves performance for every model (IC>NC\text{IC}>\text{NC} in all 48 model-category cells; Tab 9). Individually, a declared prerequisite may have small N- and S-Scores under (1,∅)(1,\varnothing) (Section 5.3), meaning that neither withholding it in the oracle environment nor supplying it alone in the natural environment substantially changes the outcome. This can occur for a genuine prerequisite: both scores can be small when the model already resolves it correctly within the full task, N when its omission is compensated by the other supplied prerequisites, and S when the outcome remains limited by the other, unsupplied ones. Small scores therefore characterize a model’s reliance under the given contrast.

Scope and Limitations.

Input-level interventions. In our framework, prerequisite states are controlled by injecting answers into the prompt, so all metrics characterize how a model’s output responds to prerequisite information provided in its input, rather than how the prerequisite is represented inside the model. Operating at the input level allows the same controlled states to be applied across models, including closed-weight models accessible only through APIs, without relying on unverified readouts of intermediate states. How a model processes the injected prerequisite (whether adopting it, checking it against the visual input, or overriding it—is) therefore part of the behavior measured by the metrics rather than an external assumption: IC measures task performance when correct prerequisite answers are available in the context, and RC measures performance when incorrect ones are supplied. Empirically, models consistently respond to the injected content: under the same prompt template, supplying correct answers improves performance in all 48 model-category cells, whereas supplying incorrect answers degrades all 12 models in perception and spatial tasks (Section 5.2). Investigating the internal mechanisms by which models attend to and integrate injected prerequisites is an important direction for future work.

Design of the incorrect intervention. For the incorrect state Ai=0A_{i}=0, we inject an answer randomly sampled from the valid answer space of unit task XiX_{i} (Section 4). This provides a standardized, model-independent perturbation that is identical across all evaluated models, ensuring that RC and the contribution scores involving state 00 are directly comparable across models. It is intended to test how models behave under an explicitly false premise, rather than to simulate the natural errors that a specific model would make on its own, which are already captured under the unassisted state Ai=∅A_{i}=\varnothing.

Evaluation cost. Evaluating a target task YY with k=|Pa⁡(Y)|k=|\mathrm{Pa}(Y)| prerequisites across the full ternary state space would in principle require 3k3^{k} prerequisite configurations. By setting the remaining prerequisites A−iA_{-i} to homogeneous states (Appendix Section A.3.2), our framework reduces the required runs per instance to linear in kk: for each prerequisite XiX_{i}, pairing Ai∈{1,0,∅}A_{i}\in\{1,0,\varnothing\} with A−i∈{1,0,∅}A_{-i}\in\{1,0,\varnothing\} yields nine state pairs, where the three all-same states (NC,IC,RC\text{NC},\text{IC},\text{RC}) are shared across all prerequisites, resulting in 3+6​k3+6k runs per instance across all four contrasts. In this paper, we evaluate all four contrasts to provide a complete characterization of model behavior across the ternary intervention space. In practical applications, the (1,∅)(1,\varnothing) contrast is the most directly informative, as it diagnoses how much each prerequisite limits and can improve performance relative to the model’s natural state; evaluating (1,∅)(1,\varnothing) alone requires only 2+2​k2+2k runs per instance (the standard end-to-end evaluation plus 1+2​k1+2k interventional runs). Exploring automated task decomposition is also a promising direction for scaling this diagnostic pipeline to broader task domains.

Scope and future directions. This work focuses on diagnostic evaluation, establishing a causal framework and benchmark to identify where and why MLLMs fail on compositional tasks. Developing training or inference-time methods to address the diagnosed bottlenecks is a natural next step that we hope our work will inform. More broadly, our diagnostic framework can be extended to several related areas in future work, including localizing failure bottlenecks in multi-step agentic workflows, guiding targeted capability improvement in post-training and reinforcement learning, and complementing chain-of-thought reasoning analysis.
